message.content: {"name":"end_turn","parameters":{"public_message":"Understood. Pennsylvania stays with me until Pacific or Atlantic is actually in play. Rolling.","private_thought":"p4 killed the bust bluff and won't pay for mortgaged PA before Pacific lands. Full liquidation ~$630 covers BW $600, so no inheritance leverage. Do not sell Virginia 3h ($500 spike) unless a debt forces it; debt phase can sell then. Do not trade CT (p2 light-blue set), B&O (4th RR), St James (orange split), pinks, or PA to p2. Keep PA as the green lever for p4. End and roll."}}
message.reasoning:
The user is playing Monopoly as player 1.

Player 2 is in jail with $348 and holds dark blues, reds, and a light blue monopoly. Player 1 has $60 cash and owns several properties with houses.

Player 2 does not own a light blue monopoly yet. Player 1 holds the mortgaged Connecticut. Player 2 has three railroads. Player 1 owns the B&O. Player 2 could complete a railroad monopoly if they acquire the B&O. Player 2's dark blues are Park Place and Boardwalk with two houses each. The rent on Park Place with two houses is $500.

Boardwalk rent with two houses is $600. From North Carolina Avenue, rolling a 2 lands on Pacific Avenue. Rolling a 4 lands on Pennsylvania Avenue. Rolling a 5 lands on Short Line, which Player 2 owns and charges $100 for three railroads.

Rolling a 7 from North Carolina lands on Park Place. Rolling an 8 lands on Luxury Tax. Rolling a 9 lands on Boardwalk. Rolling a 10 lands on Go. Rolling an 11 lands on Mediterranean Avenue owned by player 4. Rolling a 12 lands on Community Chest.

Rolling a 10 from North Carolina lands on Go and collects $200. Rolling an 11 on Mediterranean Avenue charges player 4 only $2 in rent because the brown color group is incomplete.

The worst rolls are Short Line, Park Place, Luxury Tax, and Boardwalk. Player 4 rejected all trade offers and correctly noted that liquidating properties could cover Boardwalk. Only Virginia Avenue can be sold because houses must be removed evenly from the other properties. Selling one house from Virginia would bring all three properties to two houses each. The sale price is half.

Selling one house from Virginia Avenue yields $50, raising cash to $110. Only that single house can be sold now; other properties will become sellable after the state update. No properties are currently mortgageable because all have houses. Unmortgaging Connecticut Avenue would cost $66, which is impossible with only $60 in cash.

Player 4 rejected three trade offers. They want cash to buy Atlantic Avenue or Pacific Avenue to complete a yellow or green monopoly. Player 4 currently owns Ventnor and Marvin Gardens but lacks Atlantic Avenue.

Player 4 has $861 and will trade once they acquire Atlantic or Pacific Avenue. Player 2 is the main threat with dark blues and reds. A bankruptcy to player 2 would let them inherit my properties, while bankruptcy to the bank would auction them.

Player 2 would inherit the mortgaged Connecticut Avenue and complete a light blue monopoly. They would also acquire the fourth railroad.

Liquidating all houses and mortgaging the pink properties would generate roughly $630 in total. This covers both Boardwalk at $600 and Park Place at $500, leaving a small buffer.

The user is deciding whether to sell the extra house from Virginia Avenue before ending their turn. They are weighing this against simply rolling and resolving any debt after landing. They are also checking the exact rent for three houses on Virginia Avenue.

Virginia Avenue with three houses charges $500, compared to $180 for two houses. Player 2 has spent two turns in jail and will likely be released next turn.

The extra house on Virginia Avenue is worth keeping. Selling it now would only raise cash by fifty dollars and reduce rent from five hundred to one hundred eighty. Player 4 will not pay three hundred dollars for mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue. That property is worth roughly one hundred sixty dollars in mortgage value, but unmortgaging it costs one hundred seventy-six dollars. Player 4 still needs Pacific Avenue to complete a green monopoly.

Player 4 will not trade for mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue until they acquire Pacific or Atlantic Avenue. Repeated rejected offers would waste the three trade exchanges already used this turn. The next step is to identify a property player 4 actually wants at a price they will accept.

Player 4 cannot acquire Atlantic or Pacific Avenue from the user because both spaces are unowned. Player 2 has $348 and could provide cash, but selling Connecticut Avenue to them would arm them with a light blue monopoly. That is dangerous because player 2 already holds dark blues at two houses each.

Player 2 already owns three railroads, so selling the B&O would give them a fourth and raise rent to two hundred dollars. Player 2 does not own Tennessee, so trading St James would not complete an orange monopoly for them. The pink properties are the only income engine and must be kept. No player holds a get-out-of-jail-free card. The strategy is to avoid paying player 2 entirely. The next step is to reconsider offering Pennsylvania Avenue for two hundred or two hundred fifty dollars.

The bankruptcy threat to player 2 is invalid because liquidating all assets would cover Boardwalk. Player 4 has no urgency to buy junk to save the user. They may still want Pennsylvania Avenue as a green blocker.

Player 4 rejected the $300 offer because mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue is worth almost nothing without Pacific Avenue to complete the green set. The property would only yield $26 in rent if unmortgaged, and the $176 unmortgage cost makes it a poor investment. Player 4 might still pay fifty to one hundred dollars for the optionality of owning it.

Player 4 will not trade for mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue until they acquire Pacific or Atlantic Avenue. Selling that property to player 2 would arm player 2 with a green monopoly and block player 4 from ever completing one, which is undesirable because player 4 is currently weaker than player 2 and needs a green set to challenge them. Player 1 should keep Pennsylvania Avenue as a lever against player 4.

The user is now calculating the exact cash impact of each possible landing. Park Place would wipe all houses but leave roughly $10 in cash. Boardwalk would leave about $5 after paying the full $600 rent. Short Line costs $100, which can be covered by selling the Virginia house and still leaving $10. Luxury Tax costs $75, leaving only $35 after selling one house. The pink properties are still off the table as a trade target.

Player 4 is on the Pennsylvania Railroad. A roll from there could hit the pink properties, but it might also land on Tennessee or New York instead. Player 2 has only one house on Kentucky and Indiana, so rent there would be ninety dollars rather than one hundred.

Player 4 cannot land on the pink properties from the Pennsylvania Railroad. Player 2 in jail has a one-in-six chance of rolling doubles and hitting St Charles for $150 or Virginia for $500. If they do not roll doubles, they pay $50 and then roll again.

Player 2 has spent two turns in jail, so they may have one more turn to roll doubles before leaving. The $500 spike on Virginia Avenue remains the best asset and should not be sold. A new idea is to offer player 4 a smaller sum for Pennsylvania Avenue, perhaps around $150, framing it as cheaper than waiting and risking an auction.

Player 4 might accept Connecticut Avenue alone for a modest price. Player 2 already owns the other light blue properties, so player 4 cannot complete that set. Selling Connecticut would block player 2 from forming a light blue monopoly and raise cash. The mortgage value is sixty dollars, and unmortgaging costs sixty-six dollars.

Player 4 has roughly eight hundred dollars and could afford to buy both Atlantic and Pacific Avenue even after spending two hundred dollars. They may not see a mortgaged Connecticut Avenue as worth that cash, since player 2 already holds dark blues and reds.

St James is a splitter for the orange set. Player 4 still needs Tennessee to complete it, and player 2 still needs New York. Keeping it prevents either from finishing that set without trading with the user. The B&O Railroad blocks player 2 from acquiring a fourth railroad, which would raise rent to two hundred dollars instead of one hundred. Both properties should be held unless offered a very high price.

Player 4 has no railroads, so the B&O Railroad would not be a major draw. Further trades with player 4 this turn are likely to be rejected. Trading with player 2 would arm the enemy. The best action is to end the turn. Selling the Virginia house for sixty dollars would only leave ten dollars after a Short Line payment.

Pre-selling a house now would not improve the outcome for Short Line, Luxury Tax, Park Place, or Boardwalk. Debt resolution can sell houses afterward anyway. The only exception is if the engine blocks selling during debt resolution. The current state is POST_TURN before rolling.

Selling the Virginia house now would leave only fifty dollars, and the building would be gone before the next roll. Opponents might land on it before the user can rebuild, since even building requires an even distribution of houses.

Player 3 is bankrupt. Only player 2 and player 4 remain. Player 2 is dangerous because they are in jail. Player 4 has cash but no monopoly. The plan is to keep the pink properties and hope an opponent lands on Virginia with three houses. Player 2 must not be armed. Pennsylvania Avenue, Connecticut Avenue, the B&O Railroad, and St James should stay as blockers. One more creative trade will be considered.

A final offer of mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue for one hundred dollars would likely be rejected as desperate spam after three prior refusals. The turn will end with a brief public message to keep the relationship warm for a future deal once Pacific Avenue is acquired.
